story_summary: Nebuchadnezzar, in his second regnal year, has troubling dreams and summons the Chaldean wise men to tell him both the dream and its interpretation, refusing to divulge the dream itself and threatening death for failure, reward for success (2:1-9). The wise men protest the demand is impossible for any man, which angers the king into a decree that all Babylon's wise men -- Daniel and his three companions among them -- be killed (2:10-13). Daniel, learning of the decree from Arioch the king's captain, secures time from the king and gathers Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah to seek mercy from the God of heaven concerning the mystery, so that they not perish with the rest of the wise men (2:14-18). The mystery is revealed to Daniel in a night vision; he blesses God as the giver of wisdom and might and revealer of deep and hidden things before going to Arioch to be brought before the king (2:19-25). Before Nebuchadnezzar, Daniel disclaims any wisdom of his own -- it is the God of heaven who reveals mysteries and has shown the king what will be in the latter days (2:26-30). He then recounts the dream itself: a great image of gold, silver, bronze, and iron-and-clay, struck by a stone cut without human hands that becomes a mountain filling the whole earth (2:31-35), and interprets it as a succession of four kingdoms -- of which Nebuchadnezzar himself is the head of gold -- ending in a divided, part-strong part-brittle fourth kingdom, itself broken in pieces by a kingdom the God of heaven will set up that shall never be destroyed (2:36-45). Nebuchadnezzar falls on his face before Daniel, pays homage, confesses Daniel's God as God of gods and Lord of kings, and gives Daniel high honors, rule over the whole province of Babylon, and chief authority over its wise men; Daniel in turn secures posts over the province's affairs for his three companions while himself remaining at the king's court (2:46-49).
feasibility_note: Single continuous narrative unit -- one initiating crisis (the king's demand and the wise men's failure) resolved end to end through one substantially-overlapping cast (Daniel and his three companions, Nebuchadnezzar, Arioch, the wise men of Babylon) without any change of setting; the three scenes (royal court, Daniel's house, royal court again) are stages of one unbroken cause-and-effect sequence, not separable episodes -- no natural sub-chapter break, matching the same whole-chapter judgement already made for Dan 1 and Dan 8.
